## Intro to Today's Lab

During today's lab, you'll apply the concepts discussed during this week's lecture. Each lab consists of a range of tasks, with corresponding questions you can answer. Please note that the questions are not required and not marked, although they do provide a helpful source of formative feedback that will help you gauge your understanding. 

### Learning Objectives
At the end of this lab, you will be able to:

1. Identify hypotheses which may be tested using Factorial ANOVAs
2. Run power analyses for Factorial ANOVAs
3. Check assumptions for Factorial ANOVAs
4. Use jamovi to perform Factorial ANOVAs
5. Interpret and report results from Factorial ANOVAs

## Study Overview
In this week's lab, you'll be working with data simulated based on [this paper](https://d1wqtxts1xzle7.cloudfront.net/92405721/vrtherapy-libre.pdf?1665701596=&response-content-disposition=inline%3B+filename%3DVirtual_Reality_Exposure_Therapy_for_the.pdf&Expires=1723672793&Signature=ceCWXs2EIQsAqYQSz5XM5-rSYxHeEbUHIDYv8cXqDjMrFK6~6PO-5bD05ku0EWCSZaCFaKHER1atUcfjFGUASRZ6L5aij5dBBtF~HV7f3QH70Diq~2P4MXCA5KMJYq9tWPWv4My7b~T5vLnSWGHDI9XYFfEqg7dMPBibKUtaiVTmVekzvXVQwt~E4m0cuVcA1j6KLe3nC6kfGRbO20EMfVZeCLW6f-3M5K3gr~xPnnQBjX7V3m97pJ6FoY8S9SbJzJQiyIGYe1DIh0BIYx-cV7O-a9D~Je8fQrg1wNmBhWdTLJu4h6m3SIop9B-HSTIcW0LmHlxp2SltefXxHSRukA__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAJLOHF5GGSLRBV4ZA). In this study, researchers tested the effectiveness of a virtual reality-based exposure therapy to treat PTSD in victims of the September 11th attacks. Participants were given the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS) and assigned to either a waitlist or treatment group. After the treatment group completed therapy, all participants were once again administered the CAPS.

In order to determine the effectiveness of the treatment, the following three effects must be tested:

**Main Effect 1:** Is there a significant difference in CAPS scores of PTSD patients between the treatment and waitlist groups?

**Main Effect 2:** Is there a significant difference in CAPS scores of PTSD patients between baseline and follow-up sessions?

**Interaction Effect:** Does the effect of time on CAPS scores of PTSD patients change depending upon treatment group?


You can download the data for this week's lab [here.](https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/ANOVA2lab.csv)

This dataset contains the following variables:

```{r, echo = F}
dat <- read.csv('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/ANOVA2lab.csv')
datInfo <- data.frame(VariableName=colnames(dat), 
                      Description=c('Age in years', 'Sex', 'Levels: 0 = Waitlist; 1 = VR Therapy', 'pre-intervention CAPS score (possible values = 0-80)', 'post-intervention CAPS score (possible values = 0-80)', 'CAPS score at 6 month follow-up'))

datInfo %>%
  kbl(col.names=c('Variable Name', 'Description')) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = F) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = T, color=baseColor, font_size = 18, align='l') %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = T, width = '4.5cm')
```

Here, you have 2 independent variables: Time (Baseline vs Follow-Up) and Treatment Group (VR Therapy vs Waitlist)."),
     question("What kind of variable is Treatment Group?",
              answer("Between-Subjects", correct = T),

     question("What kind of variable is Time?",

### Your Tasks

<div class="nobullet">

+ [ ] $\ $ Identify your independent and dependent variables for this experiment. 
+ [ ] $\ $ State your hypotheses for this experiment, both using words and statistically.

</div>

Note that the research questions have already been specified, above.
<br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>

To state hypotheses statistically, you should structure them in the framework of the statistical values being tested.

</details>
</div>
</br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>

<br>

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt">Variables</span>

<b>Independent Variables:</b> Time (2 levels: Baseline/Follow-up); Treatment Group (2 levels: Waitlist/VR Therapy)

<b>Dependent Variable:</b> CAPS score

<br>

<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt">Hypotheses:</span>

**Main Effect 1**

There will be no effect of Treatment Group on CAPS Score

$H_0: \mu_{waitlist} = \mu_{VRtherapy}$

<br>

There will be an effect of Treatment Group on CAPS Score

$H_1: \mu_{waitlist} \neq \mu_{VRtherapy}$

<br>

**Main Effect 2**

There will be no effect of Time on CAPS Score

$H_0: \mu_{baseline} = \mu_{post-treatment} = \mu_{follow-up}$

<br>

There will be an effect of Time on CAPS Score

$H_1:$ At least one of the following is true:

$\mu_{baseline} \neq \mu_{post-treatment}$
$\mu_{baseline} \neq \mu_{follow-up}$
$\mu_{post-treatment} \neq \mu_{follow-up}$

<br>

**Interaction**

$C = (\mu_{waitlist}\times\mu_{baseline}-\mu_{waitlist}\times\mu_{post-treatment}-\mu_{waitlist}\times\mu_{follow-up})-$
$(\mu_{treatment}\times\mu_{baseline}-\mu_{treatment}\times\mu_{post-treatment}-\mu_{treatment}\times\mu_{follow-up})$


The effect of Time on CAPs score will not dependent upon Treatment Group.

$H_0: C = 0$

<br>

The effect of Time on CAPS score is dependent upon Treatment Group.

$H_1: C \neq 0$



</details>
</div>
</br>


## Power Analysis
<br>

Recall the effect size measure for ANOVA, $\eta^2$:

```{r, echo = F}

eta2Tab <- data.frame(Strength = c('Weak', 'Moderate', 'Strong'), Magnitude = c(.01, .06, .14))

eta2Tab %>%
  kbl(col.names=c('Variable Name', paste('Magnitude of', "$\\eta^2$"))) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = F) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = T, color=baseColor, font_size = 16, align='l') %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = T, width = '4.5cm')
```

When multiple independent variables are included in the model, partial $\eta^2$ is used instead. It can be interpreted with the same thresholds.


### Your Task
For all power analyses, use $\alpha$ = .05, power = .8, and a moderate effect size ($\eta^2_p$ = .06)

<div class="nobullet">
+ [ ] $\ $ Run an a priori power analysis to determine the sample size necessary to detect the main effect of `TherapyGroup` on CAPS score. 

+ [ ] $\ $ Run an a priori power analysis to determine the sample size necessary to detect the main effect of `Time` on CAPS score. 

+ [ ] $\ $ Run an a priori power analysis to determine the sample size necessary to detect a moderate interaction effect between `TherapyGroup` and `Time` on CAPS score. 


</div>



```{r cyrPower, echo = FALSE}
quiz(caption = 'Check Your Results',
    question_numeric("How many participants do you need to detect a moderate interaction effect with 80% power and alpha = .05?",
                      answer(79, correct = T),
                      message = "You would need 79 total participants to detect the interaction effect, given the above constraints."))

```


<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>

Consider whether your independent variables are between-subjects, within-subjects, or a mix. This will impact which power analysis options you choose. Typically when reporting, it is sufficient to perform a power analysis for the most complex model (or the one for which you expect the weakest effect), as this will require the largest sample. However, on this course, you should perform a power analysis for each effect.

</details>
</div>
</br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>
<br>


<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Interaction Effect </span>

Navigate to *Power>Factorial Designs*

**Main Effect 1**
Set $\eta^2_p$ = .06. Remember that the degrees of freedom for the effect is calculated by:

$$k-1$$
where $k$ = the number of groups. Here, the degrees of freedom = 1. The design is 'Between-subjects', and the number of groups = $k$. Ensure power = .8 and $\alpha$ = .05. If you've entered all parameters properly, you should get the following results:


```{r, echo = F, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_ME1power.png')
```

**Main Effect 2**
$\eta^2_p$, power, and $\alpha$ remain the same. There are 3 levels in $IV_2$, so the degrees of freedom are now equal to 2. The design is within-subjects, and the number of groups is equal to 1. This power analysis is only for main effect 2, so 'Effect is only within' should be selected. Once all parameters have been entered, you'll get the following results:


```{r, echo = F, fig.align='center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_ME2power.png')
```

**Interaction Effect**
As before, $\eta^2_p$, power, and $\alpha$ remain the same. You'll need to keep 'Within-subjects' design selected, because at least one effect is within-subjects. To calculate the degrees of freedom for the interaction effect, use the following equation:

$$(K-1)\times(J-1)$$
where $K$ is the number of levels in $IV_1$ and $J$ is the number of levels in $IV_2$:

$$(2-1)\times(3-1) = 2$$
The total number of groups is equal to the number of levels in the between-subjects variable. Once you've entered everything properly, you should see the following results:


```{r, echo = F, fig.align='center', out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_intPower.png')
```

Here, the interaction effect actually requires fewer participants than the between-subjects main effect! However, it's because an interaction effect is rarely as strong as a main effect, so using a moderate effect threshold here may be overestimating. It is probably better to lower the expected effect size when running a power analysis for an interaction.

</details>
</div>

## Primary Analysis

In this step, you'll be checking assumptions and then running the formal analysis.

The requirements/assumptions of a Factorial ANOVA are:

(1) **Normality:** Residuals are normally distributed

(2) **Independence of Observations:** Individual observations should not be dependent upon any others

(3) **Homogeneity of Variance/Sphericity:** Variances within each level combination should be generally similar

(4) The dependent/outcome variable must be continuous and the independent/predictor variables must be categorical

### Your Tasks

<div class="nobullet">

+ [ ] $\ $ Assess and/or consider how to handle each assumption of a Mixed Factorial ANOVA

+ [ ] $\ $  Run a Mixed Factorial ANOVA to test your hypothesis and interpret the results with $\alpha$ = .05.

+ [ ] $\ $ Compute the effect sizes associated with your analysis

</div>

```{r cyrFacAOV, echo = FALSE}
quiz(caption = 'Check Your Results',
     question_numeric("What is the F-statistic associated with the main effect of Therapy Group? Please round your answer to two decimal places.",
              answer(7.87, correct = T),
              message = "The F-statistic associated with this test is 7.87."),
     question("Is the main effect of Time significant?",
              answer('Yes'),
              answer('No', correct = T),
              message = "The p-value associated with Time is .056, which is larger than the alpha threshold of .05, indicating the effect of Time is not significant."),
     question_numeric("What is the effect size (partial eta-squared) associated with the interaction effect? Please round your answer to two decimal places.",
              answer(0.06, correct = T),
              message = "The effect size associated with the interaction effect is 0.06."),
     question('True or False: No assumptions were violated.',
              answer('True'),
              answer('False', correct = T),
              message = 'This is false; although most assumption held, the assumption of sphericity was violated.')
     )
```



<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>

Have a look at the [lecture slides](https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Lectures/ANOVAII_lecture.html) if you're lost.

You'll need to fit the ANOVA model in order to check the assumptions of normality and homogeneity. Because there is a within-subjects effect included in this model, navigate to *Analyses>ANOVA>Repeated Measures ANOVA*. 


</details>
</div>
</br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>

Navigate to *Analyses>ANOVA>Repeated Measures ANOVA* and set up the model structure. In the 'Repeated Measures Factors' box, highlight 'RM Factor 1' and change the label to 'Time'. Highlight each level and change the name to the variable names (e.g. Baseline). Each time you change a level name, a new possible level will be added, so you can continue adding levels until all 5 are represented. Once this is done, drag the corresponding variables into their places in the 'Repeated Measures Cells' box. Add `TherapyGroup` to the 'Between Subject Factors' box. If you've done this properly, the set-up should look like this:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_modSetup.png')
```


*Normality*

To check the assumption of normality, scroll down to the 'Assumptions Checks' drop-down tab and tick 'Q-Q Plot'. 

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='60%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_QQplot.png')
```

The points on the Q-Q plot follow the diagonal closely, suggesting the data are distributed in the way that is expected for a normal distrubtion. 


<br>


**Independence**

This is handled through good study design. For the purpose of this example, it can be considered to be met.

<br>

**Homogeneity of Variance**

To check homogeneity of variance for the between-subjects variable, select 'Homogeneity Test' in the 'Assumptions Checks' tab. All values of $p$ are > .05, which suggests the assumption of homogeneity of variance is met.

**Sphericity**

As with Levene's test, the null hypothesis of Mauchly's test is that the assumption of sphericity is not violated, so a non-significant result ($p$ > .05) suggests we can consider this assumption to be met. Unfortunately, $p$ < .001, which suggests sphericity is violated.

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_mauchly.png')
```

Because there is a violation of sphericity, a correction must be applied to the model results. Use the flow chart below to decide what correction must be applied:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaI_sphericity.png')
```

Based on your decision, you will deselect 'None' from the 'Sphericity Corrections' box and select either 'Greenhouse-Geisser' or 'Huynh-Feldt' based on the decision made using the flow chart above.

Note that if Sphericity is not violated, you could just use the default results.


**Evaluating Factorial ANOVA Results**

Under 'Effect Size', select 'Partial $\eta^2$'. Scroll to the post-hoc tests tab and add the `Time` and interaction variables to the box on the right. You don't need to conduct a post-hoc test for `Treatment` as it only has 2 levels. To visualise and gather descriptive data for the interaction, scroll to the 'Estimated Marginal Means' tab and add **both** variables included in the interaction to the 'Term 1' box. Scroll down and make sure both 'Marginal means plots' and 'Marginal means tables' are checked.

If you've done everything properly, you should see the following results:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_modResults.png')
```

The within-subjects main effect of time is not significant, but the between-subjects main effect of therapy group is. The interaction effect is also significant, indicating that the effect of study time-point on CAPS score changes depending upon treatment group. You can also evaluate the strength of the effect of each of these variables according to the associated thresholds for $eta^2$.

Because there is a significant interaction, check the post-hoc results. The first section of results compare the CAPS at baseline to all other possible combinations of therapy group and time. 

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='85%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_intResultsBaseline.png')
```

These results indicate a significant difference in CAPS scores between the waitlist group and baseline and the therapy group post-treatment. There's also a significant difference between the treatment group's baseline scores and their scores post-treatment and at follow-up. 

The second section compares the CAPS at follow-up to the remaining combinations of therapy group and treatment.

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='85%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_intResultsPost.png')
```

There is a significant difference between the waitlist and treatment group at Post-Treatment. There is also a significant difference in the waitlist group at post-treatment and the therapy group at follow-up. Finally, there is a significant difference between the therapy group post-treatment and the waitlist group at follow-up.

The last comparison shows the difference between the therapy and waitlist groups at follow-up. This comparison is not significant.

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='85%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_intResultsfollowUp.png')
```

You can also check the visualisation and descriptive data to get a clear picture of the direction of these differences:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_intPlot.png')
```


```{r, echo = F, fig.align= 'center', out.width='75%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_EMMs.png')
```

Altogether, the results suggest that the effects of the therapy improved symptoms immediately post-treatment, but did not extend to the 6 month follow-up period.


</details>

## Interpret & Report 

Now that you've completed the analyses, write a mini results section describing your findings. In this section, please:

+ Give a brief description of your sample as you would in a methods section. 

+ Report your results and a provide interpretation in APA style. 


<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>

There are many ways you could write this up, but you'll need to at least include the following information:

+ alpha level
+ power analysis information (including effect size, sample size, power, and alpha)
+ number of participants (n)
+ participant demographics (mean age, age sd, and age range of sample; gender distribution of sample)
+ results from assumptions checks
+ descriptive data for each IV group (M and SD)
+ the type of test used
+ power analysis results
+ independent and dependent variables tested
+ type of independent variables (between- or within-subjects)
+ $F$-statistic
+ degrees of freedom
+ p-values
+ effect sizes
+ post-hoc results for any significant effects

When reporting a factorial ANOVA, you should specify the ANOVA as a JxK Factorial ANOVA, where J reflects the number of levels in your first independent variable, and K reflects the number of variables in your second independent variable.

Remember that the proper style of reporting the results from an ANOVA looks like this:

$F$([between groups $df$], [within groups $df$]) = [$F$-statistic], $p$ = [$p$-value], $\eta^2$ = [$\eta^2$ value].

Note that the numbers inside the curly brackets refer to the degrees of freedom. ANOVA has two types of $df$ that should be reported. Please refer to the [lecture slides](https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Lectures/Week06_ANOVAII_lecture.html) for a specific example.

</details>
</div>
</br>


## Bonus Material: ANCOVA

Sometimes, there may be variables that are not directly relevant to your main analysis, but may still have an effect on the dependent variable. For example, a study that is looking at how phone usage affects attention span in children and adolescents may control for age. This is because it is well-established that one's attention span changes as they age, so the researcher would want to be sure that their results reflect the true relationship between phone use and attention span, rather than age and attention span.

Variables that may have an influence on the dependent variable, but are not part of your primary analysis are called **covariates**. You can control for covariate effects by including them in your model. One model that can be used in this way is called **ANCOVA**, or Analysis of Covariance. 

### Your Task

<div class="nobullet">

+ [ ] $\ $ Run an ANCOVA by adding `Age` as a covariate to the 2x2 ANOVA model you've been working with in this lab (with `Time` and `TherapyGroup` as IVs and CAPS score as the DV). 

</div>

<br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for a hint </span></summary>

To do this, it requires a very simple update to your original model. If you'd like, you can select the output from your original results and edit the model you already created.

</details>
</div>
</br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>

To run an ANCOVA with a model with a within-subjects variable, navigate to *Analyses>ANOVA>Repeated Measures ANOVA*. Set up your IV and DVs as before (see the solution in [Primary Analysis] if you're unsure about this step). After you've added your variables, add `Age` to the 'Covariates' box:

```{r, echo = F, fig.align='center', out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_ANCOVAsetup.png')
```


You'll see that `Age` has been added to the results tables. 

```{r, echo = F, fig.align='center', out.width='50%'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/anovaII_ANCOVAresults.png')
```

If you compare the results of your key variables (`Time` and `TherapyGroup` on CAPS score), you'll notice that the values have changed slightly, but the effects have remained the same. There is still a significant effect of `TherapyGroup`, and there is still a significant interaction. However, the numeric results are slightly different. This is because these results reflect the effect of your IVs on your DV, when `Age` is held constant. In other words, you're controlling for the effect of `Age`. 

While in this case, the results did not change much, sometimes the effect of a covariate can drastically alter the model results. You should always carefully consider which covariates are important to include when planning your study and analysis, as this could have a major impact on your final outcome.

When interpreting results from ANCOVA, you should focus on the variables about which you've hypothesised (i.e., your IVs and DV). It's okay to briefly report whether or not your covariates are significant, but they should not be a strong focus of your results/discussion, and you only need to report the $p$-values. If there is a strong covariate effect and you think this has affected your hypothesised results, you might consider discussing it further in the discussion section, but it should be done in the context of your research aim and hypothesis. 

</details>
</div>
</br>

## Bonus Material: Interpret a Results Section

To answer these questions, please refer to [Difede et al., 2007.](https://www.academia.edu/88432898/Virtual_Reality_Exposure_Therapy_for_the_Treatment_of_Posttraumatic_Stress_Disorder_Following_September_11_2001)

```{r resultsSection, echo = FALSE}
quiz(caption = '',
     question_numeric('How many participants were enrolled in the study?',
              answer(21, correct = T), 
              message = '21 participants were enrolled in the study (Treatment = 13; Waitlist = 8). Athough 25 total were evaluated, 4 were excluded.'),
     question_numeric('What was the average age of participants in the treatment group?',
              answer(40.92, correct = T),
              message = 'The average age of participants in the treatment group was 40.92.'),
     question('Which of the following best reflects the design of the study?',
              answer('Between-Subjects'),
              answer('Within-Subjects'),
              answer('Mixed', correct = T),
              message = 'This is best described as a mixed design. This study included both a within-subjects variable (time: pretreatment, posttreatment), and a between-subjects variable (treatment group: waitlist, virtual reality therapy)'),
     question_numeric('What was the effect size of the interaction between time and treatment group on the CAPS score?',
              answer(0.40, correct = T),
              message = "The effect size associated with the interaction between time and treament group is 0.40"),
     question_numeric("What was the mean CAPS score in the treatment group at 6 month follow-up?",
              answer(27.3, correct = T),
              message = 'The mean CAPS score in the treatment group at 6 month follow-up was 27.3.'),
     question('Which of the following is true? Please select all that apply.',
              answer('There was a significant difference in baseline CAPS scores between the treatment and waitlist groups'),
              answer('The residual degrees of freedom in the interaction model for CAPS score is 1'),
              answer('For the waitlist group, there was no significant difference in CAPS scores between timepoints', correct = T),
              answer('There is a large effect of the interaction between time and treatment on CAPS scores', correct = T),
              random_answer_order = T,
              message = 'There was no significant difference in baseline scores between the treatment and waitlist groups. The residual degrees of freedom in the interaction model is 16. In the waitlist group, there is no significant difference in CAPS scores betweet timepoints. The eta-squared associated with the interaction effect is 0.40, which is considered a large effect.'))

```
